title: Full deduction for a totally disabled Veteran
summary: Indiana deducts 100 percent of the assessed value of your home if you have a total disability, served at least 90 days and were honorably discharged. The disability does not have to be service connected.
eligibility: You served in the military or naval forces of the United States for at least 90 days

The disability is evidenced by a pension certificate or an award of compensation issued by the US Department of Veterans Affairs, or a certificate of eligibility issued by the Indiana Department of Veterans Affairs
You own the property, or are buying it under a recorded contract that makes you liable for the property taxes, on the date the statement is filed
You have resided in Indiana for at least one year before the assessment date you are claiming for
details: Read condition three carefully, because it is more generous than most states. The statute requires a total disability. It does not require that the disability be service connected, unlike the separate partial disability deduction which does.
It covers real property, a mobile home not assessed as real property, and a manufactured home not assessed as real property, so it is not limited to conventional houses.

A surviving spouse can receive the deduction if the Veteran satisfied the service, discharge and disability conditions at the time of death, and the spouse meets the ownership condition when the statement is filed. The spouse qualifies whether or not the property was owned by the Veteran before death.
A surviving spouse loses the deduction on remarrying.
If you sold the property under a contract that makes the buyer liable for the property taxes, you cannot claim this deduction against it.
The one year Indiana residency requirement is easy to miss if you have recently moved to the state.
agency: County auditors, with certification from the US Department of Veterans Affairs or the Indiana Department of Veterans Affairs

title: Deduction for a Veteran with a partial disability, expiring in 2028
summary: Indiana deducts $24,960 of assessed value for a wartime Veteran with a service-connected disability of 10 percent or more. Act on this: the section expires on 1 January 2028.
expiryNote: The statute states that this section expires on this date. Unless the legislature extends it, the window is closing.
eligibility: You served in the military or naval forces of the United States during any of its wars
You have a service-connected disability of 10 percent or more

The disability is evidenced by a pension certificate, an award of compensation, or a disability compensation check from the US Department of Veterans Affairs, or a certificate of eligibility from the Indiana Department of Veterans Affairs
You own the property, or are buying it under a recorded contract that makes you liable for the property taxes
details: The expiry is the thing to act on. The statute states that this section expires 1 January 2028. Unless the legislature extends it, the window is closing, so claim it now if you qualify.
The 10 percent threshold is low, so many Veterans who assume they do not qualify for anything will qualify for this.
Note the difference from the total disability deduction: this one requires wartime service and a service-connected disability, while the total disability deduction requires neither.

Beginning with taxes assessed in 2026 and payable in 2027, an individual receiving this deduction may not also receive a local property tax credit under IC 6-1.1-51.3. Work out which is worth more before choosing.

There is a separate and very narrow provision giving a surviving spouse a $18,720 deduction where the deceased spouse served before 12 November 1918 and was honorably discharged. In practice that is a First World War provision and will apply to almost nobody now.
statuteRef: IC 6-1.1-12-13, with the surviving spouse provision at 6-1.1-12-16

title: Military pay and retirement deductions
summary: Indiana deducts the first $5,000 of military service pay, and from 2022 deducts military retirement and survivor benefits in full. The phase-in that capped the retirement deduction is now complete.
amount: $5,000 of military service pay, plus a full deduction of retirement and survivor benefits from tax year 2022
eligibility: The first $5,000 of income received for service in an active or reserve component of the armed forces of the United States is deducted

That covers the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, Coast Guard, Marine Corps, Merchant Marine, Indiana Army National Guard and Indiana Air National Guard, plus the Public Health Service and NOAA Commissioned Corps
Retirement or survivor's benefits for that service are deducted separately
A surviving spouse may claim either deduction in the individual's place
details: The retirement deduction reads awkwardly because the phase-in language is still in the statute. It is the lesser of the benefits included in your adjusted gross income, or $6,250 plus a percentage of the benefits above $6,250. That percentage was 25 percent in 2019, 50 percent in 2020, 75 percent in 2021, and 100 percent for taxable years beginning after 2021.
So from tax year 2022 onward the deduction equals the whole benefit. Any guidance still quoting a percentage or a $6,250 ceiling is describing a superseded year.
The two deductions are separate, so military pay and military retirement are handled under different subdivisions.
You cannot take this deduction for qualified military income that you already subtracted from federal adjusted gross income under the separate provision at IC 6-3-1-3.5(a)(18). No double counting.
